Composite: Northumbria Police and Violence against women and girls Two UK men convicted of putting explicit content on OnlyFans without consent Separate criminal convictions come as domestic violence charities warn of tech-facilitated abuse and coercion Amelia Gentleman Sat 22 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 08.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two men have been convicted this week in separate criminal cases that revealed they had posted explicit content on OnlyFans without the full consent of the women whose images were uploaded. In the first case, Alexander Tang, 37, took and uploaded 47 intimate images and four videos of a woman to OnlyFans, without her consent, and was paid money for the material he posted to the website. In the second case, a court heard how Dean Holmes, 43, had coerced a woman to open an OnlyFans account to make money. He pleaded guilty to assault and controlling and coercive behaviour at the start of the trial on Monday, but denied charges of rape. He was found guilty of rape on Thursday at the end of a four-day trial. The cases follow warnings from several domestic violence charities that some women have been compelled to create content to upload to the site. In its 2026 annual report, Women’s Aid said the most common new form of tech-facilitated abuse its frontline teams were assisting with involved “young women being coerced to set up an OnlyFans account to generate income for their abusive partners”. The Revenge Porn Helpline also said it had handled reports from women who had been coerced into creating content for OnlyFans and similar platforms. View image in fullscreen The website OnlyFans allows users to upload images and videos and monetise the content. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters During Holmes’s rape trial, Bolton crown court heard that he had isolated his victim from her family and friends and coerced her to open an OnlyFans account. Mark Kellet, prosecuting, said: “She said he put pressure on her to start making money on OnlyFans, a website where people pay for intimate content. She said that he pushed her into that. She would upload pictures of herself and the defendant would use the account to engage in text conversations with the men.” The court heard that Holmes had set the account up in her name and operated it from his phone. She had initially posted pictures of herself in a bikini, but he told her she needed to upload much more explicit content. She later told him that she felt ashamed after these images had been circulated on the site. She messaged him to say: “I can’t show my face after putting myself out there showing everything … I can’t go back to work cos people will know and people seen me advertising myself.” Holmes is due to be sentenced on 25 September. Tang pleaded guilty to one count of voyeurism and was given a 26-week suspended prison sentence on Wednesday. His victim discovered what had happened after being contacted by several men who thought they had been speaking to her on social media and dating apps; she had no idea she was on these sites. She later discovered the profiles had images of her, some naked, taken without her permission or knowledge. When she realised that the pictures had also been posted on OnlyFans, she contacted Northumbria police. Their investigations confirmed that Tang had been selling these non-consensual images, with the money going straight into his bank account. Tang had managed to take a photograph of the woman’s ID to create an OnlyFans account. The company later removed the images during a routine content moderation check. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, says equalities minister Read more In a statement she read out to the court at Tang’s sentencing hearing, his victim said: “I cannot get the images, the videos, or the degrading captions and comments associated with them out of my mind. Knowing that intimate images and videos of me were uploaded to dozens of websites, reposted and shared by strangers, is something I struggle with every day.” Alex Pattinson, the investigating officer, said: “I am horrified by Alexander Tang’s crime, which is a clear violation of this woman’s expectation of privacy. No one should ever experience what this woman has gone through – and to then learn Tang was profiting from his deceitful offending must have been devastating.” An OnlyFans spokesperson said: “OnlyFans has a zero tolerance policy for illegal content and invests heavily in measures to prevent our platform being abused in this way, including strict onboarding processes, payment controls and ongoing account moderation. We work closely with law enforcement and are proud of the work we do to support investigations and help secure convictions.” Refuge, the UK’s largest domestic abuse charity, said its staff had supported a number of survivors “with cases which involve the weaponisation of OnlyFans by perpetrators”. Speaking earlier this summer about the charity’s concerns generally (rather than in relation to these two convictions) Emma Pickering, who leads Refuge’s tech-facilitated abuse and economic empowerment team, said: “While OnlyFans already requires creators to submit proof of consent at the point of upload, for survivors to be properly protected from harm it is essential that this is robustly implemented and monitored.” Explore more on these topics Violence against women and girls Digital media Crime Social media Domestic violence news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.salisburyjournal.co.uk/news/.text: COLUMN Entertainment Music Salisbury Young Royal Academy pianists to perform in Salisbury Entertainment Music Salisbury By Poppy Byerley Share 0 Comments Farley Music Festival is a hallmark of the calendar year for Salisbury (Image: Supplied) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. As a community, Salisbury and its surrounding areas have always fostered young people and music. We have our world-famous Cathedral choristers, most of whom are local. While our schools and organisations, such as Salisbury Area Young Musicians, SAYM, produce impressive musical talent. The opportunities for young people to develop their skills are a point of pride for this little city. With so many of these opportunities, the Salisbury community has been given space to grow around our young people and classical music. Farley Music Festival is a hallmark of the calendar year for Salisbury, with its largest event taking place at the beginning of summer. Its core aim has always been to introduce the younger generations to classical music, and to allow up-and-coming performers a chance to display their talents and add to their professional experience. Read more Festival of classical music over five days Renowned classical musicians for festival concerts 'Showcasing talented musicians' - Festival near Salisbury enters 20th year OPINION: Arts in the city is on the up with launch of the new Creative, says MP John Glen Festival promises classic music thrill As the festival grew bigger in both reputation and size, Farley Music Festival spread its wings and ventured from the village into the city, with Farley Music in the Close, a series of 3 concerts performed in one day from up-and-coming international young musicians. On October 10 the festival is bringing 3 exemplary young performers to the Medieval Hall; a selection from the best students at London’s Royal Academy of Music which will allow our Salisbury community to glimpse the future of classical performance. They will each be showcasing a piano repertoire made up of classical music’s biggest names, including Mozart, Debussy, Chopin and Liszt. ‘Farley Music in the Close’ is set to be a fantastic day of professional-level performances. The day series starts at 11am with Anelise Gamulescu, a Romanian pianist, will be performing, hailed by critics for her exceptional playing and refined sound. She made her solo debut 4 years ago at the Romanian Athenaeum in Bucharest. At 2pm, Hayden Miller, who previously featured on the BBC, has chosen music spanning from the baroque period with Couperin, to the impressionist era with Debussy. The day concludes at 5pm with Özel Gunhanler. She began playing at 5 years old and has since won first prize at the 2024 Elite Musicians Competition in Romania. She is supported by the 'Upbringing of Extraordinary Children in Fine Arts' scheme by the Turkish republic of Northern Cyprus – where she was born. It's a win-win. The young performers get a chance to show off their talents and skills to a new audience. We in Salisbury get to see them for a fraction of the price we would pay in London, free for children and just £10 for adults and the city continues its tradition of encouraging musical excellence. Photograph: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP/Getty Images Flydubai plane incident Flydubai captain describes blocking axe blows as co-pilot attacked him Capt Smit Machchhar said he screamed for help as he reached to open the cockpit door on flight FZ1073 Reuters Sun 18 Oct 2026 18.27 BST Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 20.29 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The captain of a flydubai flight who was attacked by a co-pilot who intended to crash the plane has described ⁠blocking axe blows to his head and screaming for help as he reached to open the cockpit door. Capt Smit ⁠Machchhar has been hailed ⁠as a ​hero for his role in averting disaster on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month, helping to thwart what the UAE ⁠attorney general has said was an attempted suicide attack by the co-pilot who had intended to crash the plane into Ben Gurion airport. Speaking in an interview with ⁠The National newspaper from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, his head and left arm bandaged, Machchhar ​said that when the first blow landed ‌he thought something had gone “horribly ‌wrong with the aircraft structure”, before quickly realising he was being attacked and things had “taken a drastic turn”. “The ‌next thought was I need to get help in here,” he said. “My immediate action was to free myself from the seatbelts and I tried to just block the blows as much as I could.” He pointed to his arm, which had been wounded as he defended himself. “The blows were coming on the head. Immediately my ‌hand went to the knob which opens the door and [I was] screaming for my colleagues, screaming his name. I believe that was the first time when I ​lost my consciousness.” View image in fullscreen Dubai’s crown prince, sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, visited Machchhar in hospital in Abu Dhabi. Photograph: Government of Dubai Media Office/AP Flight FZ1073 was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a crash axe, an item typically kept in the cockpit for emergency use. The incident caused the airliner to plunge 16,000 ft (4,900m) in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were ⁠on board landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia . The suspect, an Omani ​national, was transferred to the ​UAE, flydubai’s home country. The plan was ​inspired by the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US, UAE public prosecutors ​said as a ‌result of their criminal ​investigation, which was launched on ​1 October. Machchhar said he heard the cockpit door opening and screaming “between my colleague and the guy”. He said the scariest moment was when he felt was the aircraft nose “steeply going down”. “I was not very sure that I’ll make it out alive from this. Did I give up?
